sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Nnw** ​(*nun*) — ‌The Primeval ‌Waters ​· The ​inert one, ​waters ​— belongs ​to the ‌Egyptian ​tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Primordial ​Waters". ‌The name ​means "The ​inert ​one, waters"[^1].

​**Nnw** — ​Nun ‌— is ​not ‌a god ​of things ‌but ​of the ‌nothing before ​things: ‌the dark, ​inert, life-teeming ​water ‌that existed ‌before creation ‌and ​surrounds the ​world still. ‌Every ​cosmogony begins ​in him; ‌every ​temple’s holy ​lake is ‌his ​miniature; and ‌every year ​the ​Nile’s flood ​re-stages his ​one ‌eternal act ‌— potential ​flooding ‌into form.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ​the ‌canonical scholarly ‌spelling **Nnw** ‌and ‌serves its ​temple at ‌[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/nun/). The ​displayed form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description computed ​from the ‌displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ‌form *nun* ​contains the ‌same ​letters: no ‌recovered diacritics ​or ‌special encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested ​in Hieroglyphs ​as ​**𓈗**. ​Etymologically ​it ‌means ​"The ​inert ‌one, waters"[^1].

​The ‌canonical ​spelling ‌**Nnw** ​matches ​the ​conventional ​scholarly romanization. ​The ‌plain ​ASCII ‌form ​*nun* ‌contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ‌no ​lost ​diacritics ‌or ‌encoding ‌transition ​is claimed. ​The ‌editorial ​work ​is ‌to ​fix ​one ‌reviewed reference ​spelling, ‌preserve ​capitalization ​and ​provenance, ​and ‌keep ‌the original ​evidence ‌visible. ​The ​displayed ‌form ‌is ‌ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description ‌computed ​from ​the ​displayed ‌form ​itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**n** ​→ ​**N** ‌— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- **u** ​→ ‌**n** ​— ‌Special ‌phonetic ​character
- ​**n** ​→ **w** ​— ‌Special ‌phonetic ​character

sections.body:
**Nnw** ​— Nun ‌— ‌is not ​a ​god ​of things ​but ​of the ‌nothing ​before things: ​the ‌dark, inert, ​life-teeming ‌water ​that existed ‌before ​creation and ​surrounds ​the world ​still. ​Every cosmogony ‌begins ​in ‌him; every ​temple’s ‌holy lake ​is ‌his miniature; ​and ‌every year ​the ​Nile’s ‌flood re-stages ‌his ‌one eternal ​act ​— potential ‌flooding ​into form.[^1]

### ​The ‌Primeval ​Water

The ​chaos-flood ‌from which ​the ‌first mound ​— ​and ​every creator ​— ‌emerged.

### Bearer ‌of ​the Mound

‌He ​lifts the ​ben-ben: ‌the ‌primeval hill ‌on ‌which the ​creator ‌stood to ​speak ​the world.

### ​The ‌Ogdoad ​Pair

With ​Naunet ​he heads ‌the ​eight frog- ​and ​snake-headed forces ‌of ​primordial ‌inertness.

### Surrounding ​Ocean

‌The world ​floats ‌in him ‌as ​a bubble ​in ​a ​flood; beyond ‌the ‌horizon, Nun ​resumes.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Nnw ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ‌set of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ​name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Primeval ​Water** ‌— ​The ‌chaos-flood ​from ‌which the ​first ‌mound ​— ‌and ​every ​creator ‌— ‌emerged.
- ‌**Bearer ​of ​the ‌Mound** ​— ​He ‌lifts ​the ​ben-ben: ‌the primeval ​hill ‌on ​which ​the ​creator ​stood ‌to ‌speak ​the ‌world.
- ​**The ​Ogdoad ‌Pair** ‌— ‌With ‌Naunet ​he ‌heads the ​eight ​frog- ​and ‌snake-headed ​forces ​of ​primordial ‌inertness.
- ​**Surrounding ​Ocean** ​— ‌The ​world ‌floats ​in ‌him ​as a ‌bubble ‌in ​a ​flood; ​beyond ​the ‌horizon, ‌Nun ​resumes.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Nun’s mythology ​is Egypt’s creation mythology ‌seen from the ‌water’s side. He ​never acts — that ​is his nature, ​and the meaning ​of his name, ‘the ​inert one’ — ‌but everything that acts, ​acts upon or ​out of him. ‌The creator gods of ​every temple city ‌are alike in ​one thing: they stood ‌on Nun’s surface ​and spoke.[^1]

### The Ogdoad ​and the First ​Mound (Hermopolitan Cosmogony)

​At Hermopolis the theology ​ran: four frog-headed ‌males and four ​snake-headed females — Nun ‌and Naunet, Huh ​and Hauhet, Kuk and ‌Kauket, Amun and ​Amaunet — swam ‌in the primordial water ​until their inertness ‌ripened into an ​egg, or a lotus, ​or the first ‌mound. From that the ‌sun rose. Nun ‌heads the eight ​because water is first ​among the inert ‌things.[^2]

### The Word ​Upon the Waters (Memphite ​Theology)

The Shabaka ‌Stone’s Memphite account has ​Ptah conceiving the ​world in the ‌heart and speaking it ​on the primeval ‌waters: creation as ​a command uttered over ​Nun. The theology ​made the water the ​page and the ‌god’s tongue the ‌pen — the deepest ​Egyptian metaphor for ‌creation as articulation.

### ​The Sea That Holds ​the Barque (Solar ‌Books)

In the underworld ‌books the sun’s ‌night barque sails ‌the *Nun* beneath the ​world — the ‌primeval water is ​also the water below, ​the source of ​renewal. At dawn the ‌barque re-emerges from ​Nun’s eastern flood: ​every sunrise is a ​re-creation, every night ‌a return to ​the uncreated.

### The Inundation ​as Epiphany (Flood ​Theology)

The Egyptians called ‌the annual flood ​simply ‘the arrival’; ‌its waters were Nun ​revisiting the world, ‌refertilising the mound. ​Temple holy lakes and ‌the ‘Ocean of ‌the Temple’ pools staged ​the same theology ​in architecture: a ​miniature primeval water at ​the god’s door, ‌in which purity ‌and creation are the ​same act.
